title: Cap. IV open: Arminianorum sententia — from Pontiffs to interpolators; Arminius on faith foresight
latin: Cap. IV. Arminianorum sententia exponitur, atque argumenta refelluntur. Omissis atque rejectis Pontificiorum argumentis, cum iis deinceps agendum est, qui interpolarunt hanc controversiam, mutatis quibusdam vocabulis, et loquendi formulis, ipsa tamen errorum fundamenta retinuerunt. In his principem locum obtinet Jacobus Arminius, vir doctus et acri ingenio, sed qui parum tribuebat antiquae Ecclesiae judicio, nihil Reformatae. Is igitur, ne crassus nimis videretur in constituenda sua defensione, noluit tueri ullum hominem praedestinari ex praevisis operibus aut meritis (ut loquuntur quidam) sed ex fide praevisa; noluit etiam quod illi de operibus audacter afferebant, de hac fide asserere, illam esse causam praedestinationis nostrae ad gloriam: sed vocabulis emollitis, docet esse tantum conditionem, aut quiddam decenter antecedaneum.
pass_a: Chapter IV. The Arminians' sentence is set forth, and their arguments are refuted. The Pontiffs' arguments having been omitted and rejected, we must next deal with those who have interpolated this controversy, certain vocabularies and forms of speaking having been changed, yet the foundations of the errors themselves having been retained. Among these Jacobus Arminius holds the chief place, a learned man and of sharp genius, but who assigned little to the judgment of the ancient Church, nothing to the Reformed. He therefore, lest he seem too crude in constituting his defense, was unwilling to maintain that any man is predestinated from foreseen works or merits (as some speak) but from foreseen faith; he was unwilling also to assert of this faith what they boldly affirmed of works, that it is the cause of our predestination to glory: but with softened words he teaches that it is only a condition, or something decently antecedent.
pass_b: Cap. IV. The Arminians' position is set out and their arguments refuted. Pontiff arguments omitted and rejected, we next deal with those who interpolated this controversy — changing some words and phrases while keeping the same error foundations. Chief among them is Jacobus Arminius: learned, sharp-minded, yet little regard for the ancient Church's judgment and none for the Reformed. Lest his defense look too crude, he would not hold anyone predestinated from foreseen works or merits (as some say) but from foreseen faith; nor would he boldly call that faith the cause of our predestination to glory as they did of works — with softened words he calls it only a condition, or something decently antecedent.

lemmas.gloss: foreseen faith as condition not cause

title: Cap. IV open: same if the thing itself is viewed — Causa/Merita; Arminius should not deny motive
latin: Verum si res ipsa spectetur, eodem redit utraque sententia, statuitque ex humano aliquo actu antecedente dependere, quod quivis a Deo praedestinetur ad vitam aeternam, aut non praedestinetur. Neque mihi videntur antiqui Patres, aut Scholastici in hac controversia Causae, imo Meriti vocabulo aliam notionem subjecisse quam hanc, ut scilicet innuant quemvis bonum actum, virtute gratiae Divinae ab homine praestitum, cujus intuitu Deus dat ex decreto sive ordinatione sua quodvis beneficium. Si igitur Deus intuitu fidei nostrae praedestinat, intuitu infidelitatis non praedestinat, negare non debuit Arminius fidem a se poni rationem vel causam motivam praedestinationis nostrae, imo meritoriam, ex phrasi et sensu antiquorum. Sed haec obiter.
pass_a: But if the thing itself is viewed, both sentences come to the same, and it is established that it depends on some antecedent human act, that anyone is predestinated by God to eternal life, or is not predestinated. Nor do the ancient Fathers, or the Scholastics in this controversy, seem to me to have subjected another notion to the word Cause, nay Merit, than this, namely that they hint any good act performed by a man by the power of Divine grace, in view of which God from his decree or ordination gives any benefit. If therefore God predestinates in view of our faith, and does not predestinate in view of unbelief, Arminius ought not to have denied that faith is by him posited as a reason or motive cause of our predestination, nay a meritorious one, from the phrase and sense of the ancients. But these things by the way.
pass_b: But if you look at the thing itself, both positions come to the same: it makes anyone's predestination (or non-predestination) to eternal life depend on some antecedent human act. The ancient Fathers and Scholastics in this controversy seem to me to mean by Cause — nay Merit — nothing else than any good act a man performs by divine grace, in view of which God by his decree or ordination grants any benefit. So if God predestinates in view of our faith and does not in view of unbelief, Arminius should not have denied that he posits faith as a reason or motive cause of our predestination — even a meritorious one, in the ancients' phrase and sense. But that by the way.

lemmas.gloss: both positions come to the same

title: Cap. IV open: duplex decretum — general (all believers) and singular (named from foreseen faith)
latin: Praedestinatione ergo hunc in modum ex praevisione fidei constituta, duplex Praedestinationis decretum ab Arminio, ejusque sectatoribus stabilitur. Prius generale est, quo Deus decrevit omnes credentes in gratiam recipere propter Christum, eosdemque in fide perseverantes aeterna vita donare. Posterius singulare est, et ad singulares personas terminatur: Quo Deus statuit hunc et illum nominatim, puta Petrum, Paulum, Johannem, quos ab aeterno praevidit credituros, et in fide permansuros, aeterna gloria donare.
pass_a: Predestination therefore having been constituted in this manner from foresight of faith, a double decree of Predestination is established by Arminius and his followers. The prior is general, by which God decreed to receive all believers into grace for Christ's sake, and to gift the same persevering in faith with eternal life. The latter is singular, and is terminated at singular persons: By which God established to gift with eternal glory this one and that one by name, for example Peter, Paul, John, whom from eternity he foresaw would believe, and would remain in faith.
pass_b: With predestination thus set from foresight of faith, Arminius and his followers establish a double decree. The first is general: God decreed to receive all believers into grace for Christ's sake, and to gift those persevering in faith with eternal life. The second is singular and terminates on particular persons: God established to gift with eternal glory this one and that by name — Peter, Paul, John — whom from eternity he foresaw would believe and remain in faith.

title: Cap. IV open: general decree urged as Scriptural — Resp. ad articulos, Hippolytus, Hague Remonstrants
latin: Est autem observatu dignum, prius illud generale decretum, quod neminem singulariter ad salutem designat, urgeri tamen maxime ab Arminio, et obtrudi pro illa praedestinatione, quam sacra Scriptura nobis commendavit. Sic in Responsione sua ad articulos, artic. 4. Hoc decretum (loquitur de isto generali et indeterminato) dico esse fundamentum Christianismi, salutis, et certitudinis de salute; deque illo agi ad Rom. 8, 10, 11. et primo capite ad Ephesios. Idem plane docet in Epistola ad Hippolytum, in qua illam praedestinationem, qua Deus dicitur decrevisse singulares quasdam personas salvare et fide donare, quasi rem parvi momenti, et in sacris Scripturis minime fundatam, transilit. Remonstrantes autem in Collatione Hagiensi, plane immemores particularis cujuscunque decreti, eo dirigunt argumenta sua, ut probent hoc unicum decretum, quo Deus indiscriminatim statuit, velle se quoslibet in fide perseverantes servare, iram vero super omnibus incredulis effundere, esse totum et integrum decretum Praedestinationis, pag. 62.
pass_a: But it is worthy of observation that that prior general decree, which designates no one singularly to salvation, is nonetheless urged most by Arminius, and thrust forward for that predestination which sacred Scripture has commended to us. So in his Response to the articles, article 4: This decree (he speaks of that general and indeterminate one) I say is the foundation of Christianity, of salvation, and of certainty concerning salvation; and that concerning it one treats at Rom. 8, 10, 11, and in the first chapter to the Ephesians. He teaches the same plainly in the Letter to Hippolytus, in which he skips over that predestination by which God is said to have decreed to save certain singular persons and gift them with faith, as a matter of small moment, and least founded in the sacred Scriptures. But the Remonstrants in the Hague Conference, plainly forgetful of any particular decree whatsoever, so direct their arguments as to prove that this sole decree, by which God indiscriminately established that he wills to save any persevering in faith, but to pour out wrath upon all the unbelieving, is the whole and entire decree of Predestination, p. 62.
pass_b: Note well: that prior general decree, which names no one singularly to salvation, is what Arminius most urges and thrusts forward as the predestination Scripture recommends. So in his Response to the articles, art. 4: This decree (the general, indeterminate one) I say is the foundation of Christianity, salvation, and certainty of salvation; and Rom. 8, 10, 11 and Ephesians 1 treat of it. The same in his Letter to Hippolytus, where he skips the predestination by which God decreed to save certain singular persons and gift them faith — as a small matter, scarcely founded in Scripture. The Remonstrants at the Hague Conference, forgetting any particular decree, aim to prove this sole decree — God indiscriminately wills to save any who persevere in faith and pour wrath on all unbelievers — is the whole and entire decree of Predestination (p. 62).

title: Cap. IV open: neither general nor foresight-singular is Pauline predestination — reply plan
latin: Nos autem e contra statuimus, neque illud generale Dei decretum in hanc formulam conceptum, Ego volo omnes in fide perseverantes servare, Neque illud singulare praescientia interveniente nixum, Ego Petrum, Paulum, Johannem, quos praevideo perseveranter credituros, aeterna vita donabo, esse eam praedestinationem de qua Apostolus in Epistola ad Romanos, ac sacrae Scripturae loquuntur. Pro posteriore hoc decreto (quod sciam) non solent pugnare adversarii, verbo asseruisse contenti: Pro priore acriter dimicant. Nos illorum argumentis primo in loco occurremus; dein sententiam nostram confirmabimus, ac contrariam eadem opera impugnabimus. Quia autem in Colloquio Hagiensi ea quae sparsim apud alios exstant argumenta, quasi in unum fasciculum comportantur, nos illorum Collocutorum objectiunculis respondebimus.
pass_a: But we on the contrary establish that neither that general decree of God conceived in this formula, I will to save all persevering in faith, Nor that singular one resting on intervening foresight, I will gift with eternal life Peter, Paul, John, whom I foresee will perseveringly believe, is that predestination of which the Apostle in the Letter to the Romans, and the sacred Scriptures, speak. For this latter decree (so far as I know) the adversaries are not accustomed to fight, content to have asserted it in a word: For the prior they contend sharply. We will first meet their arguments; then we will confirm our sentence, and by the same work impugn the contrary. But because in the Hague Colloquy those arguments which stand scattered among others are as it were gathered into one fascicle, we will answer the little objections of those Colloquists.
pass_b: We hold the contrary: neither that general decree framed I will to save all who persevere in faith, nor that singular one resting on intervening foresight — I will gift eternal life to Peter, Paul, John, whom I foresee will perseveringly believe — is the predestination of which the Apostle speaks in Romans, and sacred Scripture. For the latter decree (so far as I know) adversaries rarely fight, content to assert it in a word; for the former they contend sharply. We will first meet their arguments, then confirm our position and impugn the contrary. And because at the Hague Colloquy arguments scattered elsewhere are gathered as into one fascicle, we will answer those Colloquists' little objections.

title: Cap. IV Arg. 1: gospel-revealed will to save perseverers is the whole predestination decree
latin: Arg. 1. Voluntas Dei de salute et exitio hominum in Evangelio patefacta, est totum integrum decretum praedestinationis: Perseverantes in fide velle servare, iram vero super incredulis et impoenitentibus velle relinquere, est voluntas Dei de salute et exitio hominum in Evangelio patefacta: Ergo perseverantes in fide velle servare, iram vero super incredulis relinquere, est totum et integrum decretum praedestinationis. Majorem dicunt esse per se manifestam, nec probatione indigere; Minorem in hisce Scripturae locis expresse fundatam Joh. iii. 36, Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam; qui vero Filio non obtemperat, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super ipsum. Et Joh. vi. 40, Haec est voluntas ejus qui misit me, ut quisquis videt Filium, et credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam.
pass_a: Argument 1. The will of God concerning the salvation and ruin of men revealed in the Gospel is the whole entire decree of predestination: To will to save those persevering in faith, but to will to leave wrath upon the unbelieving and impenitent, is the will of God concerning the salvation and ruin of men revealed in the Gospel: Therefore to will to save those persevering in faith, but to leave wrath upon the unbelieving, is the whole and entire decree of predestination. They say the major is manifest of itself, and does not need proof; the minor expressly founded in these places of Scripture, John 3:36, Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. And John 6:40, This is the will of him who sent me, that whoever sees the Son, and believes in him, may have eternal life.
pass_b: Arg. 1. God's will concerning men's salvation and ruin, revealed in the Gospel, is the whole entire decree of predestination. To will to save those persevering in faith, and to leave wrath on the unbelieving and impenitent, is that gospel-revealed will. Therefore to will to save perseverers in faith and leave wrath on unbelievers is the whole and entire decree of predestination. They say the major is self-evident and needs no proof; the minor is expressly founded in John 3:36 — Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but God's wrath remains on him — and John 6:40 — This is the will of him who sent me, that whoever sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life.
